title: The Improbable Longevity of “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia”
excerpt: Paula Mejía writes about “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia.” The irreverent comedy is the longest-running sitcom in history, yet has won no major awards.
content_html:
The irreverent comedy is the longest-running sitcom in history, yet has won no major awards. What gives?

August 17, 2026

Danny DeVito, as Frank, and Glenn Howerton, as Dennis, in the first episode of Season 18.Photograph by Prashant Gupta / FX

Sometime in the mid-two-thousands, the actor Rob McElhenney sat for an on-camera interview with FX. The cable network had recently, to his palpable astonishment, green-lit a scrappy comedy that he’d shot with two friends, called “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia.” In the segment, McElhenney—scruffy, his dark-brown hair parted down the middle—explains the show’s premise: A gaggle of friends co-owns a flagging Irish bar in Philadelphia called Paddy’s Pub. McElhenney struggles to verbalize “Sunny” ’s conceit beyond that. “To get into specifics is difficult, because there is no real situation,” the newly minted showrunner says. “I mean, we find ourselves in different situations every week.” Suddenly coy, he offers, “I would say this: that if you are easily offended, you might want to not tune in.” McElhenney leaves it there, flashing a wide grin.

His vague warning undersold the degree to which “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia” entered the world deliberately courting controversy. The protagonists, known as “the gang,” cut a figure closer to frenemies than friends. They plot and scheme, sometimes together and usually at odds with one another, each driven entirely by self-interest. Notably, the show premièred, in 2005—early in George W. Bush’s second term and mere months after the début, on NBC, of “The Office,” a sacred text of the millennial hopecore era—with an episode entitled “The Gang Gets Racist.” The titular gang comprises Mac (McElhenney), a closeted wannabe tough guy; the narcissistic prepster Dennis (Glenn Howerton); Dennis’s chronically unsure fraternal twin, Dee (Kaitlin Olson); and the bar’s buffoonish janitor, Charlie (Charlie Day). Together, they hire a man from Dee’s acting class, Terrell (Malcolm Barrett), who is Black, to be a doorman at their bar as a way of proving that they aren’t racist. Terrell, who is gay and doubles as a night-club promoter, brings in scores of drinkers to their perpetually sleepy pub, transforming it into Philadelphia’s trendiest gay bar. Stunned, the gang lobs homophobic diatribes, fires Terrell, and sabotages their own success, while cluelessly reinforcing the same racism that they had defensively railed against, in addition to some reprehensible homophobia.

“Sunny,” throughout its seventeen-season run (its eighteenth season premières on August 17th), has concocted all manner of depraved schemes for its despicable antiheroes: hunting a former man of the cloth (whom they’ve driven into homelessness) for sport; locking their enemies inside an apartment that’s on fire; trying to profit from a baby they’ve found in a dumpster. Flagrantly practicing an especially ribald strain of cringe comedy that brushes several third rails, often simultaneously, the show could have been a disastrous gambit. But “Sunny” has managed to (largely) avert this fate with an act of comedic divination: it leans into ripping satire at the precise moment when the situation at hand—and, by association, the show itself—appears unsalvageable. “I think we get away with it because the characters are never rewarded,” Howerton once said in an interview. “They’re always losing. They always wind up in the same place they started in.”

Even more improbable is the fact that, by season count, “Sunny” is the longest-running live-action comedy in American TV history. (In distant second place is “The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet,” which ran for fourteen seasons.) The series has not faced cancellation in a cultural sense, even as social mores have morphed over its two decades on air. Nor has the show disappeared in a corporate bloodbath, despite substantial ownership changes at its parent company. (“Sunny” first aired on FX, then moved to anchor FX’s spinoff network FXX—targeted at younger adult audiences—when it launched, in 2013. Disney acquired Twentieth Century Fox, which included FX Networks, in 2019; several years later, it acquired a hundred per cent stake in Hulu, where the show has streamed for the better part of two decades.) It helps that the longtime head of FX, John Landgraf, is a champion of the show; when he took over the network, in 2004, Landgraf brought in edgy original programming that could be made cheaply, including “Sunny,” to rouse the struggling company. FX was one of the lowest-rated cable networks among the eighteen-to-forty-nine-year-old demographic after it débuted. Less than two decades later, Variety reported, the network was ranked sixth out of a hundred and four networks for that same age group. A few years into its run, “Sunny” also began amassing a cult fan base that tends to communicate via vocal stims of its most recognizable in-jokes.

The eighteenth season of “Sunny” hews to a familiar formula: high jinks catalyzed by ulterior motives; callbacks to long-standing bits, like Charlie (who habitually eats cat food and something inexplicably called “milk steak,” with a side of jelly beans) perhaps being a secret genius; edgy jokes about thorny cultural issues; and scenes best watched through one’s fingers, such as one in which Dee and Dennis sneak into a morgue to rip a thumb off a corpse, only to realize that the digit is from the wrong body. Viewed as a collective, the new season offers an explanation for “Sunny” ’s stubborn endurance, which has little to do with how the show inserts its finger directly into sockets. Buried within the gang’s self-absorbed pickles, petty obsessions, and moral bankruptcy is a thrum of genuine knowingness, a metatextual edge that is at its most unsparing when the show’s sights are trained on—what else?—itself.

McElhenney (who legally shortened his last name to Mac last year), Howerton, and Day first dreamed up “Sunny” when they were scraping together livings from bit parts on soap operas and procedurals. Turned off by the meagre roles that Hollywood had for them, the friends decided to make a show for laughs, about three twentysomething actors trying to make it in Los Angeles. They used Howerton and Day’s cheap digital camcorders. When they weren’t acting in front of the camera, they were behind it or holding the boom mike, learning as they went. Dubbed “It’s Always Sunny on TV,” the tape made its way to FX.

Executives loved the show’s winking humor, but worried about its familiar setting. In the early two-thousands, HBO’s roster featured three shows that addressed Hollywood’s casual cruelties: “The Comeback,” “Entourage,” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm.” NBC had invested in the “Friends” spinoff “Joey,” which followed its titular character, an actor, as he moved to L.A. So the “Sunny” team ditched that idea and changed the show’s setting to Philadelphia, where Mac had grown up. Their characters were written as night-life-industry colleagues, not actors. (The show’s revamped name, “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia,” is a pseudo joke: the sun-drenched series is shot predominantly in L.A., save for the odd episode and B-roll in its eponymous city.) The first season was filmed on a scrappy budget of four hundred and fifty thousand dollars per episode, a fraction of what it cost to make a network sitcom at the time.

The series received a lukewarm reception from critics and earned middling ratings upon its release, in August, 2005. In the Philadelphia Daily News, Ellen Gray panned “Sunny” as a show that “simply isn’t funny enough often enough to justify its rather labored envelope-pushing.” The New York Daily News was less generous, concluding that “just because you can put something on TV doesn’t mean you should.” Despite the low ratings, Landgraf liked the show—and that it cost next to nothing to make. Ahead of the comedy’s second season, FX brought on Danny DeVito to play Dennis and Dee’s impish, absentee businessman father, Frank, in hopes that his presence would bring in more viewers. (Landgraf and DeVito were two co-founders of Jersey Films, a TV-production company they started in 1999.) The inclusion of Frank, portrayed by DeVito with a rollicking sleaze, gave the writers more latitude to probe intergenerational disputes, corrosive familial dynamics, and debauchery: he has a penchant for having sex in dumpsters, he cuts his nails with an unwashed “toe knife,” and admits, at one point, to having defecated in the bed that he shares with his roommate, Charlie.

Viewership rates ticked up after FX released the show on DVD and beefed up its marketing toward college students; the show also found a niche audience on Hulu, which launched to the public in early 2008. On the cusp of the Obama era, the kind of sitcoms that were being made moved from canned network fare to cheery mockumentaries and programs stuffed with laugh-a-minute zingers. “Sunny” ’s anti-sitcom bona fides were beloved among fans who appreciated its subversive streak. But the program still continues to float somewhat under the radar, never having found massive mainstream popularity via ratings or awards—an exclusion that has not gone unnoticed by the show. An early episode features a jab that Mac directs at Dennis and Charlie which reads as a veiled comment about Hollywood’s inability to grasp “Sunny” itself: “Our problem is that we don’t stick to that basic format, and that gets us into trouble,” Mac says. “So what you’re saying is that by breaking from that format, we’re actually limiting our ability to be as successful?” Dennis asks. Another episode, in which the pals attempt to win an award for best bar, parallels the comedy’s perpetual shutout from the Emmy Awards. (It has received only three nominations, all for Outstanding Stunt Coordination for a comedy program; it has won none.) Two years ago, the actors of “Sunny” finally made it onto the Emmys stage—as presenters. “Wait, hang on, have you guys been doing this every single year without us?” Day asked the crowd from the stage. “Maybe they got some trophies backstage that they just, like, forgot to give us.”

“Sunny” frequently draws comparisons to the profane animated comedy “South Park,” which addresses Zeitgeisty tensions with a similar irreverence. The difference is that “Sunny” does not frame the issues it’s tackling as to-the-minute shocks to the status quo, as “South Park” often does. When “Sunny” introduces culture-war topics, like #MeToo, and political issues, such as gun control, it mines humor from how these topical conversations further elucidate the gang’s depravity. In one of the new episodes, for instance, Dee becomes a ruthless marketing executive who coerces her intern into sex by asking him, “Do you believe women?” Another Season 18 episode ostensibly riffs on the right’s cavalier handling and selective perception of the Epstein files, and subtly mocks vaccine skepticism when the gang insists that they “did their own research.”

To me, the closest sibling to “Sunny” is not “South Park” but, rather, “Peep Show,” a now defunct British comedy that was the longest-running program of its kind on Channel 4. Shot in an excruciating P.O.V. style, the show tracks two horribly selfish flatmates whose friendship—rooted in history and a waning sense of obligation—is best described as “lead weights dragging each other down,” as one of them puts it. When “Sunny” first aired, it zagged away from dominant sitcom hits such as “Friends,” with weekly conundrums that neither tested their characters’ friendships nor reinforced their long-standing bonds. It wouldn’t suffice to characterize “Sunny,” either, as a show about nothing except observing daily absurdities, as “Seinfeld” is. The gang never learns anything, in fact, save for new ways to be horribly cruel to one another—taking the “Peep Show” frenemy ambiguity one step further—with Dee a particularly frequent target: the others repeatedly dismiss her by calling her a “bird” and, in one of their meanest schemes, the gang tries to help her out of a depressive episode by leading her to believe that she’s finally become a star on the comedy circuit. By digging into the cruelty that reflects darker shades of our society, the show exposes it.

“Sunny” shares another, more controversial kinship with “Peep Show.” In 2020, a spate of sitcoms on streaming platforms and in syndication, including “Community,” “30 Rock,” and “Golden Girls,” pulled episodes that showed their characters using black- and brownface; likewise, FX took down five episodes of “Sunny.” The decision divided fans: some approved of the decision, whereas others advocated for the episodes’ return to streaming, so long as they included a disclaimer about the racially offensive content. In 2021, Mac addressed the controversy by stating that his “barometer is off for what’s appropriate sometimes in situations because, like, we’ve spent fifteen years making a show about the worst people on the planet, and because it’s satire, we lean so heavily into this idea.” (The episodes remain unavailable on streaming platforms.)

In a Season 15 episode, “The Gang Makes Lethal Weapon 7,” which originally aired in 2021, the show addresses its own regretful use of blackface by lampooning Hollywood’s self-congratulatory stance during the racial reckonings of 2020. After the library removes the gang’s “Lethal Weapon” tribute films (these films-within-the-show feature in some of the earlier “Sunny” episodes that have been removed from streaming) because of the blackface that Mac used in portraying Roger Murtaugh, played by Danny Glover in the original film series, the group reflects on their racism with hollow sincerity: “We’ve also done a lot of growing,” Dee says. Mac later announces that he would be “magnanimously taking a step back” from the role of Murtaugh. He stops, waiting for applause. “I’m doing something anti-racist, and I think I deserve praise for that, do I not?” The episode ends with a behind-the-scenes documentary about the gang’s making of “Lethal Weapon 7,” called “White Saviors.”

Since 2020, an ongoing cultural rejection of inclusive language and actions—exacerbated by a Presidential Administration that revels in liberal and left-leaning citizens’ anger at its intentionally cruel treatment of immigrants, people of color, and L.G.T.B.Q.+-identifying people—has seeped into our culture. The visible brutality of Trump 2.0, in a sense, has caught up to the universe that “Sunny” inhabits: a place where its characters get a clear kick out of the barbaric pains that they inflict on one another. Following a string of uneven seasons, “Sunny” ’s eighteenth outing finds fertile terrain by toying with this pronounced sociopolitical pendulum swing—but not by vindicating its characters, who, it’s implied, might share similarly cold-blooded impulses. The new episodes skewer MAGA’s desire to “own the libs” even if it’s at great cost to themselves, the movement’s rampant cultural apathy, and the false promises of nostalgic revisionist histories.

The season begins with a two-parter (spoilers ahead) about Frank marrying the billionaire Sam (Carol Kane), whom he met when the two competed on “The Golden Bachelor,” in the finale of the previous season. Sam agrees to secretly share her fortune with Dennis and Dee, so long as the wedding happens. One ill-fated bout of flesh-eating bacteria later, Sam dies—but not before Dee and Dennis, to insure that they get their cut, prop her body up at the altar so that Frank unknowingly marries her corpse. While figuring out the legal bureaucracies surrounding Sam’s money, the working-class siblings complain about their physical proximity to their broke friends. Dennis’s disdainful outcries—“We’re surrounded by poverty, Dee . . . hold your breath because you can catch it, it’s like a disease you can catch!”—poke at both the ruling class and blue-collar Americans who might vote against policies that could help ease the ill effects of corporate greed on their own lives. Although never stated outright, Dee and Dennis’s exaggerated get-rich-quick plot smacks of risky financial endeavors, such as the rise of dystopian prediction markets. And the season’s most idiotic gag, with various characters dressed up for Frank’s wedding in Colonel Sanders-esque Western black-ribbon bow ties, functions as an indictment of our culture’s complacent incuriosity: the gang would rather look ridiculous in the ribbon ties than learn how to tie a bow tie.

But the newest crop of “Sunny” episodes takes on a trenchant precision by prodding at a strain of culture that’s smitten with the fantasy of nostalgia and calls on the right to “make America great again.” In a standout new episode, “The War on Alcohol,” the gang, after lamenting that booze sales have waned at the bar, decides to bring blue- and white-collar workers together for a happy hour to remind them of alcohol’s pleasures. The scheme goes sideways, as the friends realize that the nature of work has changed, with the rise of remote jobs and automation and the decline of communal gatherings, and that culture no longer values excessive drinking—which, as they viscerally come to see, could lead to dire consequences such as injury, harassment, and death. Moreover, the narrative seems to suggest that romanticizing the past makes it no easier to trudge into an uncertain future.

One welcome surprise: a newly installed automated beer machine garners a substantial profit from non-alcoholic-beer sales. “Maybe we’re thinking about this whole thing all wrong,” Mac says, in a moment of brief clarity. “Maybe we should embrace a modern workplace environment.” But that would mean they learned something. The gang hauls the contraption to the front curb and pours their non-alcoholic beers into it. Satisfied, they head back inside the bar to find “a real beer.” Never growing, it seems, goes down as easy as a lager. ♦

While figuring out the legal bureaucracies surrounding Sam’s money, the working-class siblings complain about their physical proximity to their broke friends. Dennis’s disdainful outcries—“We’re surrounded by poverty, Dee . . . hold your breath because you can catch it, it’s like a disease you can catch!”—poke at both the ruling class and blue-collar Americans who might vote against policies that could help ease the ill effects of corporate greed on their own lives. Although never stated outright, Dee and Dennis’s exaggerated get-rich-quick plot smacks of risky financial endeavors, such as the rise of dystopian prediction markets. And the season’s most idiotic gag, with various characters dressed up for Frank’s wedding in Colonel Sanders-esque Western black-ribbon bow ties, functions as an indictment of our culture’s complacent incuriosity: the gang would rather look ridiculous in the ribbon ties than learn how to tie a bow tie.But the newest crop of “Sunny” episodes takes on a trenchant precision by prodding at a strain of culture that’s smitten with the fantasy of nostalgia and calls on the right to “make America great again.” In a standout new episode, “The War on Alcohol,” the gang, after lamenting that booze sales have waned at the bar, decides to bring blue- and white-collar workers together for a happy hour to remind them of alcohol’s pleasures. The scheme goes sideways, as the friends realize that the nature of work has changed, with the rise of remote jobs and automation and the decline of communal gatherings, and that culture no longer values excessive drinking—which, as they viscerally come to see, could lead to dire consequences such as injury, harassment, and death. Moreover, the narrative seems to suggest that romanticizing the past makes it no easier to trudge into an uncertain future.One welcome surprise: a newly installed automated beer machine garners a substantial profit from non-alcoholic-beer sales. “Maybe we’re thinking about this whole thing all wrong,” Mac says, in a moment of brief clarity. “Maybe we should embrace a modern workplace environment.” But that would mean they learned something. The gang hauls the contraption to the front curb and pours their non-alcoholic beers into it. Satisfied, they head back inside the bar to find “a real beer.” Never growing, it seems, goes down as easy as a lager. ♦

blocks.html_en: Sometime in the mid-two-thousands, the actor Rob McElhenney sat for an on-camera interview with FX. The protagonists, known as “the gang,” cut a figure closer to frenemies than friends. They plot and scheme, sometimes together and usually at odds with one another, each driven entirely by self-interest. Notably, the show premièred, in 2005—early in George W. blocks.html_en: Even more improbable is the fact that, by season count, “Sunny” is the longest-running live-action comedy in American TV history. (In distant second place is “The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet,” which ran for fourteen seasons.) The series has not faced cancellation in a cultural sense, even as social mores have morphed over its two decades on air. Nor has the show disappeared in a corporate bloodbath, despite substantial ownership changes at its parent company. (“Sunny” first aired on FX, then moved to anchor FX’s spinoff network FXX—targeted at younger adult audiences—when it launched, in 2013. Disney acquired Twentieth Century Fox, which included FX Networks, in 2019; several years later, it acquired a hundred per cent stake in Hulu, where the show has streamed for the better part of two decades.) It helps that the longtime head of FX, John Landgraf, is a champion of the show; when he took over the network, in 2004, Landgraf brought in edgy original programming that could be made cheaply, including “Sunny,” to rouse the struggling company. FX was one of the lowest-rated cable networks among the eighteen-to-forty-nine-year-old demographic after it débuted. Less than two decades later, Variety reported, the network was ranked sixth out of a hundred and four networks for that same age group. A few years into its run, “Sunny” also began amassing a cult fan base that tends to communicate via vocal stims of its most recognizable in-jokes.

blocks.html_en: The eighteenth season of “Sunny” hews to a familiar formula: high jinks catalyzed by ulterior motives; callbacks to long-standing bits, like Charlie (who habitually eats cat food and something inexplicably called “milk steak,” with a side of jelly beans) perhaps being a secret genius; edgy jokes about thorny cultural issues; and scenes best watched through one’s fingers, such as one in which Dee and Dennis sneak into a morgue to rip a thumb off a corpse, only to realize that the digit is from the wrong body. Viewed as a collective, the new season offers an explanation for “Sunny” ’s stubborn endurance, which has little to do with how the show inserts its finger directly into sockets. blocks.html_en: The series received a lukewarm reception from critics and earned middling ratings upon its release, in August, 2005. Ahead of the comedy’s second season, FX brought on Danny DeVito to play Dennis and Dee’s impish, absentee businessman father, Frank, in hopes that his presence would bring in more viewers. (Landgraf and DeVito were two co-founders of Jersey Films, a TV-production company they started in 1999.) The inclusion of Frank, portrayed by DeVito with a rollicking sleaze, gave the writers more latitude to probe intergenerational disputes, corrosive familial dynamics, and debauchery: he has a penchant for having sex in dumpsters, he cuts his nails with an unwashed “toe knife,” and admits, at one point, to having defecated in the bed that he shares with his roommate, Charlie.

blocks.html_en: Viewership rates ticked up after FX released the show on DVD and beefed up its marketing toward college students; the show also found a niche audience on Hulu, which launched to the public in early 2008. On the cusp of the Obama era, the kind of sitcoms that were being made moved from canned network fare to cheery mockumentaries and programs stuffed with laugh-a-minute zingers. “Sunny” ’s anti-sitcom bona fides were beloved among fans who appreciated its subversive streak. But the program still continues to float somewhat under the radar, never having found massive mainstream popularity via ratings or awards—an exclusion that has not gone unnoticed by the show. An early episode features a jab that Mac directs at Dennis and Charlie which reads as a veiled comment about Hollywood’s inability to grasp “Sunny” itself: “Our problem is that we don’t stick to that basic format, and that gets us into trouble,” Mac says. “So what you’re saying is that by breaking from that format, we’re actually limiting our ability to be as successful?” Dennis asks. Another episode, in which the pals attempt to win an award for best bar, parallels the comedy’s perpetual shutout from the Emmy Awards. (It has received only three nominations, all for Outstanding Stunt Coordination for a comedy program; it has won none.) Two years ago, the actors of “Sunny” finally made it onto the Emmys stage—as presenters. “Wait, hang on, have you guys been doing this every single year without us?” Day asked the crowd from the stage. “Maybe they got some trophies backstage that they just, like, forgot to give us.”

blocks.html_en: “Sunny” frequently draws comparisons to the profane animated comedy “South Park,” which addresses Zeitgeisty tensions with a similar irreverence. The difference is that “Sunny” does not frame the issues it’s tackling as to-the-minute shocks to the status quo, as “South Park” often does. When “Sunny” introduces culture-war topics, like #MeToo, and political issues, such as gun control, it mines humor from how these topical conversations further elucidate the gang’s depravity. In one of the new episodes, for instance, Dee becomes a ruthless marketing executive who coerces her intern into sex by asking him, “Do you believe women?” Another Season 18 episode ostensibly riffs on the right’s cavalier handling and selective perception of the Epstein files, and subtly mocks vaccine skepticism when the gang insists that they “did their own research.”

blocks.html_en: To me, the closest sibling to “Sunny” is not “South Park” but, rather, “Peep Show,” a now defunct British comedy that was the longest-running program of its kind on Channel 4. Shot in an excruciating P.O.V. style, the show tracks two horribly selfish flatmates whose friendship—rooted in history and a waning sense of obligation—is best described as “lead weights dragging each other down,” as one of them puts it. When “Sunny” first aired, it zagged away from dominant sitcom hits such as “Friends,” with weekly conundrums that neither tested their characters’ friendships nor reinforced their long-standing bonds. It wouldn’t suffice to characterize “Sunny,” either, as a show about nothing except observing daily absurdities, as “Seinfeld” is. The gang never learns anything, in fact, save for new ways to be horribly cruel to one another—taking the “Peep Show” frenemy ambiguity one step further—with Dee a particularly frequent target: the others repeatedly dismiss her by calling her a “bird” and, in one of their meanest schemes, the gang tries to help her out of a depressive episode by leading her to believe that she’s finally become a star on the comedy circuit. By digging into the cruelty that reflects darker shades of our society, the show exposes it.

blocks.html_en: “Sunny” shares another, more controversial kinship with “Peep Show.” In 2020, a spate of sitcoms on streaming platforms and in syndication, including “Community,” “30 Rock,” and “Golden Girls,” pulled episodes that showed their characters using black- and brownface; likewise, FX took down five episodes of “Sunny.” The decision divided fans: some approved of the decision, whereas others advocated for the episodes’ return to streaming, so long as they included a disclaimer about the racially offensive content. In 2021, Mac addressed the controversy by stating that his “barometer is off for what’s appropriate sometimes in situations because, like, we’ve spent fifteen years making a show about the worst people on the planet, and because it’s satire, we lean so heavily into this idea.” (The episodes remain unavailable on streaming platforms.)

blocks.html_en: In a Season 15 episode, “The Gang Makes Lethal Weapon 7,” which originally aired in 2021, the show addresses its own regretful use of blackface by lampooning Hollywood’s self-congratulatory stance during the racial reckonings of 2020. After the library removes the gang’s “Lethal Weapon” tribute films (these films-within-the-show feature in some of the earlier “Sunny” episodes that have been removed from streaming) because of the blackface that Mac used in portraying Roger Murtaugh, played by Danny Glover in the original film series, the group reflects on their racism with hollow sincerity: “We’ve also done a lot of growing,” Dee says. Mac later announces that he would be “magnanimously taking a step back” from the role of Murtaugh. He stops, waiting for applause. “I’m doing something anti-racist, and I think I deserve praise for that, do I not?” The episode ends with a behind-the-scenes documentary about the gang’s making of “Lethal Weapon 7,” called “White Saviors.”

blocks.html_en: Since 2020, an ongoing cultural rejection of inclusive language and actions—exacerbated by a Presidential Administration that revels in liberal and left-leaning citizens’ anger at its intentionally cruel treatment of immigrants, people of color, and L.G.T.B.Q.+-identifying people—has seeped into our culture. The visible brutality of Trump 2.0, in a sense, has caught up to the universe that “Sunny” inhabits: a place where its characters get a clear kick out of the barbaric pains that they inflict on one another. Following a string of uneven seasons, “Sunny” ’s eighteenth outing finds fertile terrain by toying with this pronounced sociopolitical pendulum swing—but not by vindicating its characters, who, it’s implied, might share similarly cold-blooded impulses. The new episodes skewer MAGA’s desire to “own the libs” even if it’s at great cost to themselves, the movement’s rampant cultural apathy, and the false promises of nostalgic revisionist histories.

content_html_zh:
这部不敬的喜剧是历史上播出时间最长的情景喜剧，但没有获得任何重大奖项。 什么给？

2026 年 8 月 17 日

第 18 季第一集中，丹尼·德维托饰演弗兰克，格伦·豪尔顿饰演丹尼斯。摄影：Prashant Gupta / FX

两千多岁的某个时候，演员罗布·麦克尔亨尼 (Rob McElhenney) 接受了 FX 电视台的镜头采访。 令他明显惊讶的是，有线电视网络最近批准了他与两个朋友拍摄的一部斗志旺盛的喜剧，名为《费城总是阳光明媚》。 在这段视频中，麦克尔亨尼——一头邋遢的深棕色头发从中间分开——解释了该剧的前提：一群朋友在费城共同拥有一家摇摇欲坠的爱尔兰酒吧，名叫帕迪酒吧。 麦克尔亨尼很难用语言来表达“Sunny”除此之外的自负。 “要了解具体细节很困难，因为没有真实的情况，”这位新晋剧集主管说道。 “我的意思是，我们每周都会遇到不同的情况。” 突然，他腼腆地说道：“我想说的是：如果你很容易被冒犯，你可能不想收听。” 麦克尔亨尼把它留在那里，露出灿烂的笑容。

他含糊的警告低估了《费城永远阳光明媚》进入世界的程度，故意引起争议。 主角们被称为“帮派”，他们的形象与其说是朋友，不如说是亦敌亦友。 他们密谋谋划，有时在一起，但通常彼此不和，每个人都完全受自身利益的驱动。 值得注意的是，该剧于 2005 年首播，当时乔治·W·布什 (George W. 布什的第二个任期和 NBC 首播的《办公室》仅几个月后，这是千禧一代希望核心时代的神圣文本，其中有一集题为“帮派变得种族主义”。 这个名义上的帮派成员包括麦克（麦克尔亨尼饰），一个想成为一名未出柜的硬汉的人；自恋的预科生丹尼斯（格伦·豪尔顿饰）；丹尼斯的异卵双胞胎迪伊（凯特琳·奥尔森饰）长期缺乏自信；还有酒吧里滑稽的看门人查理（查理·戴饰）。 他们一起从迪伊的表演班聘请了一名黑人特雷尔（马尔科姆·巴雷特饰）来担任他们酒吧的门卫，以证明他们不是种族主义者。 特雷尔是一名同性恋，兼任夜总会发起人，他为他们永远沉睡的酒吧带来了数十名饮酒者，将其改造成费城最时尚的同性恋酒吧。 震惊之余，这群人对同性恋进行了谩骂，解雇了特雷尔，破坏了他们自己的成功，同时毫无头绪地强化了他们曾经防御性地反对的种族主义，以及一些应受谴责的恐同情绪。

《阳光灿烂》在其第十七季的播出中（第十八季于 8 月 17 日首播），为其卑鄙的反英雄们炮制了各种邪恶的计划：追捕一名前富翁（他们已将他赶到无家可归）以取乐；将敌人锁在着火的公寓内；试图从垃圾箱里发现的婴儿身上获利。 公然练习一种特别粗俗的令人畏缩的喜剧风格，经常同时触碰几个第三轨，这部剧可能是一个灾难性的策略。 但《阳光灿烂》成功地（在很大程度上）通过一种喜剧占卜的方式扭转了这种命运：当眼前的情况——以及由此联想到的节目本身——似乎无法挽救时，它倾向于进行撕心裂肺的讽刺。 “我认为我们侥幸逃脱了惩罚，因为角色从未得到奖励，”豪尔顿曾在接受采访时说道。 “他们总是会输。 他们总是会回到出发的同一个地方。”

更不可能的是，按季数计算，《阳光灿烂》是美国电视历史上播出时间最长的真人喜剧。 （排在第二位的是《奥齐和哈丽特历险记》，该剧已经播出了十四季。） 尽管社会风气在播出二十年来发生了变化，但从文化意义上来说，该剧并没有面临被取消的情况。 尽管其母公司的所有权发生了重大变化，但该剧也没有在企业大屠杀中消失。 （《Sunny》首先在 FX 电视台播出，随后在 2013 年推出时，转至 FX 的衍生网络 FXX（针对年轻成人观众）播出。 迪士尼于 2019 年收购了二十世纪福克斯公司，其中包括 FX Networks；几年后，它收购了 Hulu 100% 的股份，该节目已在该网站上播放了二十年的大部分时间。） FX 的长期负责人约翰·兰德格拉夫 (John Landgraf) 是该节目的拥护者，这一点很有帮助。 2004 年，兰德格拉夫接管该电视网时，引进了一些制作成本低廉的前卫原创节目，其中包括《Sunny》，以唤醒这家陷入困境的公司。 FX 开播后是 18 至 49 岁人群中收视率最低的有线电视网络之一。 据 Variety 报道，不到二十年后，该电视网在同一年龄段的 104 个电视网中排名第六。 播出几年后，《阳光灿烂》也开始积累了一批狂热的粉丝群，他们倾向于通过其最知名的笑话的声音刺激进行交流。

《阳光灿烂》第十八季遵循了一个熟悉的套路：别有用心的狂欢；别有用心的狂欢；回想起长期存在的事情，比如查理（他习惯吃猫粮和一种莫名其妙地被称为“牛奶牛排”的东西，配上软糖豆）也许是一个秘密天才；关于棘手文化问题的尖锐笑话；最好通过手指观看的场景，例如迪伊和丹尼斯潜入太平间，从尸体上扯下一根拇指，却发现手指来自错误的尸体。 作为一个集体来看，新一季为“阳光”的顽强忍耐力提供了一个解释，这与节目如何将手指直接插入插座无关。 在这帮人的自我陶醉、琐碎的痴迷和道德败坏之中，隐藏着一股真正的知识，一种元文本边缘，当节目的目光聚焦在——还有什么？——本身时，这种元文本边缘就变得最无情。

麦克尔亨尼（去年合法地将自己的姓氏缩写为麦克）、豪尔顿和戴在靠肥皂剧和程序片的零碎谋生时首次梦想出“Sunny”。 朋友们对好莱坞为他们提供的微薄角色感到厌烦，决定制作一部搞笑剧，讲述三个二十多岁的演员试图在洛杉矶取得成功的故事。 他们使用豪顿和戴的廉价数码摄像机。 当他们不在镜头前表演时，他们会在镜头后面或拿着麦克风，边走边学习。 该录像带被称为“电视上总是阳光明媚”，并在 FX 播出。

高管们喜欢该节目的眨眼幽默，但担心其熟悉的场景。 在两千出头的时间里，HBO 的节目单上有三部讲述好莱坞随性残酷行为的剧集：《卷土重来》、《明星伙伴》和《抑制你的热情》。 NBC 投资了《老友记》的衍生剧《乔伊》，该剧讲述了演员搬到洛杉矶的故事。 因此，《阳光灿烂》团队放弃了这个想法，并将节目的背景改为费城，麦克就是在那里长大的。 他们的角色是夜生活行业的同事，而不是演员。 （该剧的改名“费城永远阳光明媚”是一个伪笑话：这部阳光普照的剧集主要在洛杉矶拍摄，除了在同名城市拍摄的奇怪剧集和幕后花絮。） 第一季的拍摄预算非常紧张，每集四十五万美元，这只是当时制作网络情景喜剧成本的一小部分。

该剧于 2005 年 8 月上映后，评论家反应冷淡，收视率中等。 在《费城每日新闻》中，艾伦·格雷批评《阳光灿烂》是一部“不够有趣的节目，不足以证明其费力的挑战是合理的”。 《纽约每日新闻》则没有那么慷慨，其结论是“仅仅因为你可以在电视上播放某些内容并不意味着你应该这样做。” 尽管收视率很低，兰德格拉夫还是喜欢这部剧，而且制作成本几乎为零。 在这部喜剧第二季开始之前，FX 电视台请丹尼·德维托饰演丹尼斯和迪伊顽皮、缺席的商人父亲弗兰克，希望他的出现能吸引更多观众。 （Landgraf 和 DeVito 是 Jersey Films 的两位联合创始人，他们于 1999 年创办了一家电视制作公司。） 弗兰克（德维托饰演的一个欢闹的下流人物）的加入，让编剧们有更多的自由度来探讨代际争端、腐蚀性的家庭动态和放荡：他喜欢在垃圾箱里做爱，他用一把没洗过的“脚趾刀”剪指甲，并承认有一次在他和室友查理同住的床上排便。

FX 电视台以 DVD 形式发行了该剧并加强了对大学生的营销，收视率有所上升；该节目还在 Hulu 上找到了小众观众，Hulu 于 2008 年初向公众推出。 在奥巴马时代的风口浪尖上，制作的情景喜剧从预先录制的电视节目转变为欢快的纪录片和充满笑点的节目。 《阳光明媚》的反情景喜剧真诚受到粉丝的喜爱，他们欣赏其颠覆性的风格。 但该节目仍然继续在某种程度上受到关注，从未通过收视率或奖项获得主流的广泛欢迎——该节目并没有忽视这一排除。 在早期的一集里，麦克对丹尼斯和查理进行了猛烈的攻击，这可以看作是对好莱坞无法理解《阳光灿烂》本身的含蓄评论：“我们的问题是我们没有坚持这种基本格式，这让我们陷入了麻烦，”麦克说。 “那么你的意思是，通过打破这种模式，我们实际上限制了我们取得成功的能力？” 丹尼斯问道。 在另一集中，伙伴们试图赢得最佳酒吧奖，这与这部喜剧永远被艾美奖拒之门外相呼应。 （它只获得了三项提名，全部是喜剧节目的杰出特技协调提名；但它没有获奖。） 两年前，《阳光灿烂》的演员们终于登上了艾美奖的舞台——担任主持人。 “等等，等一下，你们每年都在没有我们的情况下这样做吗？” 戴向台上的人群问道。 “也许他们在后台拿到了一些奖杯，只是忘记给我们了。”

《阳光明媚》经常被拿来与亵渎的动画喜剧《南方公园》进行比较，后者以类似的不敬态度解决了时代精神的紧张局势。 不同之处在于，《阳光灿烂》并没有像《南方公园》那样，将它所解决的问题描述为对现状的即时冲击。 当《Sunny》引入文化战争话题（如#MeToo）和政治问题（如枪支管制）时，它从这些话题性对话中挖掘幽默，进一步阐明该团伙的堕落。 例如，在新的一集中，迪伊成为一名无情的营销主管，她通过问实习生“你相信女人吗？”来强迫他发生性关系。 第 18 季的另一集表面上是对右翼的漫不经心的处理和对爱泼斯坦档案的选择性看法的即兴表演，当该团伙坚称他们“做了自己的研究”时，巧妙地嘲笑了疫苗的怀疑论。

对我来说，与《阳光灿烂》最接近的兄弟不是《南方公园》，而是《西洋镜》，这是一部现已停播的英国喜剧，是第四频道同类节目中播出时间最长的节目。 以令人难以忍受的视角拍摄 该剧讲述了两个极度自私的室友的故事，他们的友谊——植根于历史和日渐减弱的义务感——正如其中一位所说，最好的描述是“互相拖累的铅锤”。 当《阳光明媚》首次播出时，它与《老友记》等热门情景喜剧不同，每周都会出现一些难题，既没有考验角色的友谊，也没有加强他们长期的联系。 仅仅将《阳光明媚》描述为一部除了观察日常荒谬之外什么也没有的节目，就像《宋飞正传》一样，也是不够的。 事实上，这帮人从来没有学到任何东西，除了以新的方式彼此残忍地对待彼此——将“西洋镜”中亦敌亦友的暧昧关系进一步推向了一步——其中迪伊是一个特别常见的目标：其他人不断地称她为“鸟”而对她不屑一顾，而在他们最卑鄙的计划中，这伙人试图通过让她相信自己终于成为喜剧界的明星来帮助她摆脱抑郁的困扰。 通过深入挖掘反映我们社会阴暗面的残酷行为，该剧将其揭露出来。

《阳光明媚》与《西洋镜》还有另一个更具争议性的相似之处。 2020 年，包括《Community》、《30 Rock》和《Golden Girls》在内的一系列情景喜剧在流媒体平台和联合组织中撤下，其中的角色使用黑人和棕色面孔。同样，FX 电视台也撤下了《阳光明媚》的五集。 这一决定引起了粉丝的分歧：一些人支持这一决定，而另一些人则主张这些剧集回归流媒体，只要其中包含有关种族攻击性内容的免责声明。 2021 年，麦克在解决这一争议时表示，他的“晴雨表有时在某些情况下是不合适的，因为我们花了 15 年时间制作一部关于地球上最糟糕的人的节目，而且因为它是讽刺剧，所以我们非常倾向于这个想法。” （这些剧集在流媒体平台上仍然无法观看。）

在最初于 2021 年播出的第 15 季剧集《黑帮制造致命武器 7》中，该剧通过讽刺好莱坞在 2020 年种族清算期间沾沾自喜的立场，表达了自己对黑脸使用的遗憾。 由于麦克在原版电影系列中由丹尼·格洛弗饰演的罗杰·墨塔时使用了黑脸，图书馆删除了该团伙的“致命武器”致敬影片（这些片中影片出现在一些已从流媒体中删除的早期“阳光明媚”剧集中）后，该团体以空洞的诚意反思了他们的种族主义：“我们也做了很多成长，”迪伊说。 麦克后来宣布，他将“慷慨地退出”墨塔这个角色。 他停下来，等待掌声。 “我正在做一些反种族主义的事情，我认为我应该为此受到赞扬，不是吗？” 本集以一部关于该团伙制作《致命武器 7》的幕后纪录片《白色救世主》结束。

自 2020 年以来，对包容性语言和行动的持续文化排斥已经渗透到我们的文化中，而总统政府则因自由派和左倾公民对其故意残酷对待移民、有色人种和 L.G.T.B.Q.+ 群体而感到愤怒，加剧了这种排斥。 从某种意义上说，特朗普2.0的明显残暴已经赶上了《阳光灿烂》所居住的宇宙：在这个宇宙中，剧中的角色从彼此施加的野蛮痛苦中得到了明显的刺激。 在经历了一连串不稳定的季节之后，《阳光灿烂》的第十八部通过玩弄这种明显的社会政治钟摆找到了肥沃的土壤，但不是通过证明其角色是正确的，这暗示着他们可能也有类似的冷血冲动。 新剧集刺痛了 MAGA 想要“拥有自由”的愿望，即使这会给他们自己带来巨大的代价，该运动猖獗的文化冷漠，以及怀旧修正主义历史的虚假承诺。

本季以两部剧开始（剧透），讲述弗兰克与亿万富翁山姆（卡罗尔·凯恩饰）结婚的故事，他们是在上一季结局中两人参加“黄金单身汉”比赛时认识的。 山姆同意与丹尼斯和迪伊秘密分享她的财产，只要婚礼举行。 一场不幸的食肉细菌之后，萨姆死了——但在此之前，迪伊和丹尼斯为了确保他们得到割伤，将她的尸体支撑在祭坛上，以便弗兰克在不知不觉中与她的尸体结婚。 在弄清楚围绕萨姆的钱的法律官僚机构时，工薪阶层的兄弟姐妹抱怨他们与破产的朋友的身体距离太近。 丹尼斯轻蔑的叫喊——“我们被贫困包围了，迪…… 屏住呼吸，因为你会感染它，就像你会感染一种疾病一样！”——讽刺了美国的统治阶级和蓝领阶层，他们可能会投票反对有助于减轻企业贪婪对他们自己生活造成的不良影响的政策。 尽管迪伊和丹尼斯从未直言不讳，但夸张的快速致富情节带有冒险的金融活动的味道，例如反乌托邦预测市场的兴起。 本季最愚蠢的笑料是，不同的人物在弗兰克的婚礼上穿着桑德斯上校式的西方黑丝带领结，这是对我们文化中自鸣得意的冷漠的控诉：这帮人宁愿戴丝带领带看起来很可笑，也不愿学习如何打领结。

但最新一季的《阳光灿烂》剧集通过刺激一种充满怀旧幻想并呼吁右翼“让美国再次伟大”的文化，呈现出尖锐的精准性。 在精彩的新剧集“酒精之战”中，这群人在感叹酒吧的酒类销量下降后，决定将蓝领和白领工人聚集在一起度过欢乐时光，以提醒他们酒精的乐趣。 这个计划出了岔子，因为朋友们意识到，随着远程工作和自动化的兴起以及公共聚会的减少，工作的性质已经发生了变化，而且文化不再重视过度饮酒——正如他们本能地意识到的那样，这可能会导致可怕的后果，如受伤、骚扰和死亡。 此外，故事似乎表明，将过去浪漫化并不会让我们更容易走向不确定的未来。

一个令人惊喜的惊喜是：一台新安装的自动化啤酒机从无酒精啤酒的销售中获得了可观的利润。 “也许我们对整件事的思考都是错误的，”麦克短暂清晰地说道。 “也许我们应该拥抱现代化的工作环境。” 但这意味着他们学到了一些东西。 这伙人把这个装置拖到前面的路边，然后把不含酒精的啤酒倒进去。 他们满意地回到酒吧里寻找“真正的啤酒”。 似乎永远不会像啤酒一样容易沉下去。 ❖
